node_fields.description: A Canadian historian of family, welfare and religion whose work asks how liberal authority was made through everyday institutions. In her 2009 contribution to the liberal-order debate, Christie credits Ian McKay’s framework with connecting cultural and social research while disputing its periodization, its emphasis on the state and its property-based account of individualism. Drawing on Bruce Curtis’s distinction between liberalism and governmentality, she asks for a more precise account of power. She proposes treating churches, voluntary associations and households as places where liberal values were made and contested, so that women’s participation, not only their exclusion, becomes part of the explanation. Engendering the State (2000) and her books with Michael Gauvreau on Protestant churches and social welfare place these institutions at the centre of Canadian social history.

node_fields.description: A settler historian of Indigenous–newcomer relations, residential schooling and treaties in Canada. Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) is his history of Indian–white relations in Canada. Shingwauk’s Vision (1996), a cross-Canada history of residential schooling, shifts the focus of responsibility from the churches toward the federal government and, ultimately, Euro-Canadian society. Celia Haig-Brown’s review credits the book’s breadth and research while criticizing how examples drawn across places and decades flatten differences among nations and schools, and questioning its claims to balance and its treatment of resistance. Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009) carries his work into the history of treaty-making.

node_fields.description: A Canadian archaeologist and ethnohistorian of the Wendat (Huron) and of colonial encounters in northeastern North America. The Children of Aataentsic (1976) combines archaeology, history and ethnology to argue that Iroquoian societies had changed substantially in the centuries before European contact, so that the impact of contact cannot be assessed without understanding that earlier change. Natives and Newcomers (1985) reconsiders Canada’s ‘heroic age’ of exploration and colonization in the same way, and A History of Archaeological Thought (1989) is his history of his own discipline. He wrote the foreword to Georges E. Sioui’s For an Amerindian Autohistory (1992). Emma LaRocque criticizes that foreword as an example of containment, and argues that the cross-cultural approach to which Trigger belonged, though an improvement on earlier racist scholarship, could still distance and Other its subjects.

node_fields.description: A historian of medieval European religion, gender and the body. Holy Feast and Holy Fast (1987) argues that food lay at the heart of much late-medieval women’s piety: women renounced ordinary food through fasting to prepare for the extraordinary food of the eucharist, and offered themselves as food in miracles of feeding. Where earlier scholars had treated fasting, stigmata and inedia in isolation or through modern medical and psychological theories, she showed how these practices enabled women to exert control within the family and religious life. In ‘Why All the Fuss about the Body?’ (1995) she engages sympathetically with Judith Butler’s performative account of gender, but insists that medieval and modern ideas of body and identity be compared in their own settings; the Middle Ages, she writes, was characterized by ‘a cacophony of discourses’. Jesus as Mother (1982) and Fragmentation and Redemption (1991) are her other major collections on gender and the body in medieval religion.

node_fields.description: A medieval historian whose studies of property, immunity and power led to an influential approach to the history of emotions. ‘Worrying about Emotions in History’ (2002) revisits Lucien Febvre’s call for a history of feeling and rejects the grand narrative, associated with Norbert Elias, of a movement from unrestrained medieval emotion to modern self-control. In its place she proposes emotional communities: overlapping groups that value and express emotions in different ways. In a 2010 interview she questions William Reddy’s sharp distinction between emotional regimes and emotional refuges; Reddy’s reply allowing plural regimes stands beside her objection. Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006) is the book-length study.

node_fields.description: A historian of modern Britain, war, the body and emotion. Dismembering the Male (1996) studies men’s bodies and masculinity in the First World War. An Intimate History of Killing (1999), drawing on letters, diaries and memoirs of British, American and Australian combatants in the two world wars and Vietnam, argues that the structure of war encouraged pleasure in killing and that ordinary men could become enthusiastic killers without being brutalized. Her later work on fear and pain asks what emotions do: expressions of fear follow learned conventions yet can change the feeling they name, a point she develops through William Reddy’s concept of the emotive.

node_fields.description: A historian of early modern English beliefs, social relations and attitudes. Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) asks why beliefs in magic, astrology and witchcraft made sense in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century England and why they declined; the inquiry began, he recalls, from a puzzle about astrology and led him to anthropology. His 1963 essay ‘History and Anthropology’ grew from a review of Evans-Pritchard that Lawrence Stone encouraged him to expand. Thomas names Christopher Hill and R. H. Tawney as formative influences, and was drawn to Lucien Febvre’s inquiry into people’s assumptions rather than to quantitative Annales history. He later called his work a descriptive ethnography of early modern England and conceded that his explanation of magic’s decline was incomplete. Jan Machielsen and Michelle Pfeffer’s 2023 reassessment, building on Hildred Geertz’s criticism, questions the book’s categories of religion and magic. Man and the Natural World (1983) traced changing English attitudes to nature.

node_fields.description: A historian of early modern Spain and its empire. His first two books, The Revolt of the Catalans and Imperial Spain, 1469–1716, both appeared in 1963; a biography of the Count-Duke of Olivares followed in 1986. His interest in state formation and ‘composite monarchies’ runs from the Catalan revolt to Scots and Catalans (2018), and Empires of the Atlantic World (2006) compares British and Spanish America. Richard Kagan and Geoffrey Parker’s memoir records his admiration for Lucien Febvre’s regional synthesis and his doubts about how Fernand Braudel joined structures to events; the wish to disprove Braudel, with a belief in political biography, drove the Olivares project. His 1980 review of Carlo Ginzburg questioned how far a single case could represent a wider society. Ginzburg rejected Elliott’s opposition of micro- to macrohistory, and Natalie Zemon Davis rejected a zero-sum choice between histories of Martin Guerre and Martin Luther.

node_fields.description: A historian of empire who made its cultural presence in Britain, and its environmental history overseas, central subjects of imperial history. As founding editor of Manchester University Press’s Studies in Imperialism series he set out to examine how imperialism shaped the dominant societies as well as those they ruled; Propaganda and Empire (1984) studied the manipulation of British public opinion. The Empire of Nature (1988) connected hunting and conservation with British rule in Africa and India. Orientalism: History, Theory and the Arts (1995) challenged Edward Said’s generalizations through empirical study of the arts, as Berny Sèbe describes; Said in turn criticized an approach he associated with MacKenzie that treated culture as propaganda. His exchanges with Bernard Porter, after Porter’s The Absent-Minded Imperialists (2004), became among the most-read items in the Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History.

node_fields.description: A historian of the Dutch Republic, European Jewry and the Enlightenment whose radical-Enlightenment interpretation gives philosophical ideas a strong explanatory role. In a 2023 interview, Israel argues that the reception of Spinoza helped create a radical current committed to secularism, democratic republicanism and freedom of expression, which he opposes to a moderate Enlightenment. The coherence and reach of that current are disputed. Antoine Lilti stresses the diversity of the most heterodox Enlightenment writings and the ambiguity of ‘Spinozism’ as a historian’s category. David Bell credits Israel’s range and his insistence on ideas, but argues that he infers influence from similarity, takes passages out of context and overstates the ideological causes of the French Revolution.

node_fields.description: A historian of early modern Europe, war and the Spanish monarchy whose work connects military organization with the resources and reach of states. The Army of Flanders and the Spanish Road (1972) began as a Cambridge doctorate under John Elliott, from Elliott’s question of how Spain sustained its army in the Netherlands. The Military Revolution (1988) extended Michael Roberts’s thesis to fortification and the scale of armies, and made it an argument about the rise of the West; it has remained a debate rather than a settled explanation. Global Crisis (2013) connects the political upheavals of the seventeenth century with climatic change across regions.

node_fields.description: A historian of Scottish society, economy and diaspora. The Tobacco Lords (1975) studied Glasgow’s tobacco merchants, Clanship to Crofters’ War (1994) the social transformation of the Highlands, and The Scottish Nation (1999) is his history of modern Scotland. In ‘Did Slavery Make Scotia Great?’ (2011) he reopens Eric Williams’s question about slavery and economic development, arguing that Scotland’s stake cannot be measured by the few slaving voyages from its ports but must include the wider plantation economies. With Jenny Wormald he called for comparative, internationalized Scottish history rather than an insular national narrative.

node_fields.description: A historian of modern Germany who has also defended historical knowledge in public. In Defence of History (1997) answers the writers who brought postmodernist epistemology into historical theory; he names Hayden White, Frank Ankersmit, Keith Jenkins, Patrick Joyce, Dominick LaCapra and Beverley Southgate. He wrote it because the standard textbooks were still Carr’s What Is History? and Elton’s The Practice of History, which he found inadequate. Its introduction accepts White’s point that historians can learn from outside scrutiny of how historical knowledge is made, while rejecting Joyce’s claim that historians must accept postmodernity as an inescapable condition. Death in Hamburg (1987) connects cholera with social inequality and civic government. He served as an expert witness on the falsification of history in the 2000 Irving libel trial, and The Coming of the Third Reich (2003) began his history of Nazi Germany.

node_fields.description: A cultural historian of the body, sexuality and death. Making Sex (1990) argues that a ‘one-sex’ model, in which men and women were thought to share the same basic body, gave way in the eighteenth century to a ‘two-sex’ model grounded in biological difference: sex difference itself has a history. The thesis has been both influential and contested. Brooke Holmes, drawing on work by Katharine Park, Robert Nye, Joan Cadden and Helen King, argues that the evidence shows more varied and coexisting models, and traces the book’s narrative of epochal rupture to Foucault’s history of sexuality. Caroline Walker Bynum drew on it while noting Park and Nye’s qualification. Solitary Sex (2003) is a cultural history of masturbation, and The Work of the Dead (2015) asks what the care and naming of the dead do for the living.

node_fields.description: A historian of modern Europe and of political organization. His first book, Recasting Bourgeois Europe (1975), compares France, Germany and Italy after the First World War and argues that they did not return to the prewar order but achieved a new balance between state authority and organized interests. The Unmasterable Past (1988) addressed history, the Holocaust and German national identity. In later work he treats territoriality as a historical resource: borders, sovereignty and technologies of communication shape both government and belonging, and a networked world has not abolished the state. A conference report records John Breuilly’s challenge to the coherence of an ‘age of territoriality’, and Partha Chatterjee’s contrast with the overlapping sovereignties of Mughal India and the flexible sovereignty of colonial rule.

node_fields.description: A historian of Soviet Russia and of international relations whose What Is History? (1961) became the standard British introduction to historical method. Carr argued that historians select and give meaning to facts through their questions, so that research and interpretation proceed together; his position was long read as a challenge to objectivist history. G. R. Elton’s The Practice of History (1967) was written in open opposition, and John Tosh called the Carr–Elton controversy the best starting point for debate about the standing of historical knowledge. Richard Evans wrote In Defence of History (1997) because Carr’s and Elton’s books were still the standard textbooks and, in his view, inadequate for later debates. The Twenty Years’ Crisis (1939) belongs to his work on international relations, and his History of Soviet Russia began with The Bolshevik Revolution (1950).

node_fields.description: A historian of international power, strategy and political economy. The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers (1987) argues that great powers decline relative to others when their strategic commitments outrun their economic base; readers summarized this as ‘imperial overstretch’, and in the late 1980s it was read as a warning to the United States. Michael Cox notes that the idea was not wholly new, and Kennedy himself traced one stimulus to Mahan’s use of an earlier reflection on Spain’s dispersed empire. In the same roundtable Varsha Venkatasubramanian criticized the book’s neglect of non-state actors and of politics’ effects on economic development; Kennedy accepted her point about India and conceded that the book may contain too much economic determinism. His earlier books studied British naval mastery and the Anglo-German antagonism before 1914.

node_fields.description: A historian of Scottish society who helped establish environmental history in Scotland. A History of the Scottish People, 1560–1830 (1969) and A Century of the Scottish People (1986) are his social histories of Scotland. His 1990 British Academy lecture ‘The Highlands and the Roots of Green Consciousness’ questions the story that appreciation of Highland landscapes was simply imported into an indifferent society. In later environmental work he draws on E. A. Wrigley’s account of the shift from organic to fossil-fuel economies, and names William Cronon’s city-and-hinterland history as a model for studies of Scottish cities still to be written.

node_fields.description: A historian of South Asia, and a founding member of the Subaltern Studies collective, whose work brings medicine, science and environment into the study of colonial power. Colonizing the Body (1993) studies state medicine and epidemic disease in nineteenth-century India. The introduction to Science, Technology and Medicine in Colonial India (2000) rejects a single trajectory from European discovery to passive reception overseas. Drawing on Steven Shapin’s account of knowledge as socially situated, it insists that a history of science in India must also be a history of India. It criticizes George Basalla’s diffusion model for flattening differences among colonial situations, marginalizing local agency and assuming a beneficial sequence of development, while also rejecting accounts that understate colonial disruption. His environmental histories include The Problem of Nature (1996) and The Tropics and the Traveling Gaze (2006).

node_fields.description: An environmental historian who works at global and regional scales. Something New Under the Sun (2000) is an environmental history of the twentieth-century world. Mosquito Empires (2010) argues that ecological change made the Greater Caribbean hospitable to the mosquitoes that carry yellow fever and malaria. Because survivors gained immunity or resistance, these diseases took sides in the struggles for empire and revolution between 1620 and 1914, decimating forces sent from Europe. His survey of the field credits the Annales with an inspiring general approach while noting how little environmental history its founders wrote, and treats Alfred Crosby’s studies of ecological exchange as landmarks. In his 2020 AHA presidential address he argues that scientific evidence can illuminate histories poorly documented in writing, while warning against monocausal climate histories and against letting a new tool dictate the question.

node_fields.description: A historian of the Soviet Union and of Stalinism from below. In ‘Revisionism in Retrospect’ (2008) she gives a participant’s account of how social historians of the 1970s and 1980s challenged political scientists’ totalitarian model, crediting revisionism with an appreciation of contingency and a new approach to power and to the interplay of government and society. Stalin’s Peasants: Resistance and Survival in the Russian Village after Collectivization (1994) and Everyday Stalinism: Ordinary Life in Extraordinary Times (1999) carry that social history into village and city. In a comparative chapter with Alf Lüdtke on Nazism and Stalinism, she treats Hannah Arendt’s thesis of social atomization as a question for research: social bonds were broken but also remade, and participation involved people’s emotional investments.

node_fields.description: A medieval historian of relics, memory and ethnic identity. Furta Sacra (1978) studied thefts of relics in the central Middle Ages, and his essay ‘Sacred Commodities’ (1986) asks what made relics exchangeable within a particular medieval setting rather than assuming a timeless market. Phantoms of Remembrance (1994) concerns memory and oblivion at the end of the first millennium. The Myth of Nations (2002) uses research on changing early medieval identities to criticize modern nationalist claims to ancient continuity; Steven Fanning credits its central argument while warning that its survey contains questionable assertions and broad generalizations.

node_fields.description: A historian of cities, capitalism and environmental disaster. City of Quartz (1990) and Ecology of Fear (1998) examined the political economy and ecology of Los Angeles. Late Victorian Holocausts (2001) argues that the famines of the late nineteenth century arose from the interaction of El Niño droughts with imperial and market systems that left populations vulnerable, not from weather alone; it opens from Raymond Williams’s reflection on nature and human history. Davis recalls that Robert Brenner’s UCLA seminar on Capital, which moved on to crisis theory and twentieth-century economic history, gave him the confidence to pursue his own agenda. He later criticized Marx and Engels for saying nothing about cities and for leaving the patriarchy of the workers’ movement unchallenged.

node_fields.description: A historian of early modern Britain and Europe. His 1959 essay on ‘The General Crisis of the Seventeenth Century’, prompted, as Blair Worden notes, by Eric Hobsbawm’s Marxist analysis of the century’s revolts, set the English revolution within a wider European crisis; the later preface to his essays questions a simple Calvinism-to-capitalism explanation associated with Weber and Tawney. Worden explains his resistance to deterministic accounts of revolution, including Christopher Hill’s, and his attention to contingency and personality. In his chapter for Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger’s The Invention of Tradition (1983) he argued that the kilt, clan tartans and the very idea of a distinct Highland culture, to which Scots ascribe great antiquity, are largely modern, developed after the Union with England; The Invention of Scotland (2008) extends the theme. His authentication of the forged Hitler diaries in 1983 was a serious failure of judgment.

node_fields.description: A historian of European intellectual and cultural life who joined social history to psychoanalysis. The Enlightenment: An Interpretation (1966, 1969), Weimar Culture (1968) and the five-volume The Bourgeois Experience: Victoria to Freud (1984–98) are his major studies, and Freud: A Life for Our Time (1988) is his biography of Freud. In a 1997 interview he describes Freud as an indispensable resource for studying the interplay of psychological processes and external circumstances, insisting that an event such as the French Revolution still requires attention to state finances, royal prestige and social conflict. He criticized psychohistory that gave inner experience too much causal weight.

node_fields.description: A historian of medicine and science. The Cholera Years (1962), on the United States in 1832, 1849 and 1866, is credited with leading historians to study not only a disease and its victims but society’s response to it, through politics, law and social mores. The Care of Strangers (1987), a history of the American hospital, and Explaining Epidemics (1992) continued that social history of medicine. In a 2013 interview he places his work within a social-medicine tradition that treats medical ideas and access to care as embedded in society, questions tidy genealogies in which translated theorists alone changed historical research, and distinguishes psychiatric diagnostic categories that organize research and care from explanations of mechanism.

node_fields.description: A medieval historian of conquest, law and historical categories. Trial by Fire and Water (1986) studied the medieval judicial ordeal, and The Making of Europe (1993) traced conquest, colonization and cultural change between 950 and 1350. His 2001 article on race and ethnicity treats both terms as social constructions and warns against using present administrative labels as ready-made historical explanations. Comparing medieval terminology, he emphasizes culture, law, language and religion in the making of identities, while examining genealogical idioms of descent, and separates collective identity from any automatic demand for sovereign statehood. Geraldine Heng later questions the sharpness of his distinction between medieval cultural difference and biological racism.

node_fields.description: A literary scholar and theorist whose New Historicism reads literature within the whole field of a period’s culture. Renaissance Self-Fashioning (1980) examines how More, Tyndale, Wyatt, Spenser, Marlowe and Shakespeare fashioned selves, finding that new questions about identity shaped sixteenth-century writing. He calls New Historicism ‘madly eclectic’: it grew from impatience with American formalism and with Marxist criticism, and drew on Foucault to escape the base/superstructure dichotomy, as well as on Walter Benjamin, Michel de Certeau and Clifford Geertz. He credits Raymond Williams with showing how to connect art to the world in which it is made. Sarah Maza questions how far New Historicism and historians’ cultural history actually meet across disciplinary lines, and John Monfasani criticized The Swerve for opposing medieval darkness to Renaissance modernity; Greenblatt replied defending the Renaissance and the importance of atomism.
